$comment: Curated literals for required input members no recipe binds (docs/plans/compat-coverage-modelgen.md §3.3 rule 3). Every value must be legal on AWS, not merely accepted by the emulator; the generator checks each against the model's enum, length, range and pattern constraints. Identifiers here are syntactically valid and deliberately nonexistent — they bind probes of operations the emulator does not implement, where the call is expected to fail before the value is looked at. That is also why they are the only thing a probe may bind: a probe is the one generated call no delete undoes, so it must never name a resource the run owns.

batch.$comment: Batch is Tier 0 and every one of these binds a probe, so each value names a resource that does not exist and cannot be created by a run: no $name prefix appears in any of them, which is what keeps a probe off anything the suite owns. Two shapes are worth stating. A Batch ARN is arn:aws:batch:<region>:<account>:<resource-type>/<name> — compute-environment, job-queue, job-definition, scheduling-policy, consumable-resource and quota-share all follow it — so a quota-share ARN in the documentation account is well-formed and refers to nothing. And a Batch job id is a UUID, which is why the two job identifiers are the nil UUID rather than a word: a non-UUID is answered with a validation error rather than the not-found a probe is written for. consumableResource and jobQueue take a name or an ARN, and the name is the shorter honest answer.

iam.$comment: Identifiers of IAM objects that do not exist, all of them in the documentation account 123456789012 rather than the caller's, so no probe can reach the policy, user, role, group or instance profile a run created. Four shapes matter, because a value of the wrong shape is answered with a validation error rather than the NoSuchEntity a probe is written for. An IAM ARN is arn:aws:iam::<account>:<type>/<name>, the type spelling the object — policy, user, role, mfa, oidc-provider, saml-provider — and an OIDC provider's name being its issuer host rather than a word. An access key id is AKIA and sixteen more characters and an SSH public key id APKA and sixteen more, both of them AWS's own documentation examples. A service namespace is the prefix an IAM action is written with, so s3 is real and names nothing this run owns. And an access-advisor or organizations-report JobId is exactly 36 characters, which is a UUID — hence the nil UUID rather than a word. PolicyArn is written out on each of the three unimplemented reads that take one because the policy resource binds PolicyArn and a probe may never draw on a binding a live resource supplies; GetSSHPublicKey's UserName is the same story. Three probeable reads are deliberately left with no literal. GetRoleTemplateVersion belongs to the role-template API AWS added to the model after every released SDK: aws-sdk-go-v2/service/iam v1.53.7 declares no GetRoleTemplateVersionInput, so a literal here would scope the whole iam probe group away from go-sdk and break the java, dotnet and rust builds, which resolve an operation only at compile time. GetOrganizationsAccessReport and GetServiceLastAccessedDetails, by contrast, do get one: their JobId is minted by a Generate* call no probe may make, and a job id nobody generated is precisely the well-formed-but-nonexistent identifier every other entry here is.

kms.$comment: One key identifier, written out per operation rather than once against KeyIdType: the key resource binds KeyId, and a probe may not draw on a binding a live resource supplies, so each unimplemented read that takes a key needs its own entry. A KMS key id is a UUID — an identifier of any other shape is answered with a validation error rather than the NotFoundException a probe is written for — and the nil UUID is a well-formed key id no account holds. It carries no $name prefix, so it can never name the key the run created. GetKeyLastUsage is the fourth such read and is deliberately left refused rather than given a literal: AWS added it to the model in April 2026, and three of the four typed suites pin an SDK older than that — aws-sdk-go-v2/service/kms v1.50.4 declares no GetKeyLastUsageInput, and the rust suite's aws-sdk-kms 1.52.0 is from December 2024 — so probing it would scope the whole probe group away from go-sdk and break the java, dotnet and rust builds, which resolve the operation only at compile time. Adding the literal is the one line that reverses this once those pins move.

elastic-load-balancing.$comment: Names a Classic load balancer that does not exist. The name is 27 characters, inside AWS's 32-character limit for a load balancer name, and it carries no $name prefix, so it can never be the one a run created: DescribeLoadBalancerAttributes answers LoadBalancerNotFound for it rather than reaching anything. It needs an entry of its own because the loadbalancer resource binds LoadBalancerName, and a probe may not draw on a binding a live resource supplies. DescribeTags carried a matching entry once and must never carry one again: the loadbalancer resource's `tags` role claims DescribeTags as its list operation, and a curated LoadBalancerNames literal here would let that role bind it — against a load balancer this literal deliberately does not name, so the generated assertion would look for the run's tag on a describe of something else entirely. AddTags, DescribeTags and RemoveTags all take LoadBalancerNames, and all three get it from the recipe's own one-element-list `binds` entry instead, which aims them at the load balancer the run created.

servicediscovery.$comment: Two identifiers of Cloud Map resources that do not exist, both shaped the way Cloud Map shapes its own. A service id is `srv-` followed by sixteen lowercase alphanumerics, and an operation id is a thirty-two character token, a hyphen and eight more — the shape matters because a value of the wrong shape is answered with InvalidInput rather than the not-found a probe is written for. GetInstancesHealthStatus needs an entry rather than a binding because the service resource exports the id of a service the run owns, and a probe may not draw on that.

sns.$comment: Five identifiers of SNS resources that do not exist, in the documentation account rather than the caller's, so no probe can reach the topic the run created. Three of them are ARNs and their shapes matter: a topic ARN is arn:aws:sns:<region>:<account>:<name>, a platform application ARN is app/<platform>/<name> under the same prefix and an endpoint ARN is endpoint/<platform>/<name>/<uuid> — a value of the wrong shape is answered InvalidParameter rather than the not-found a probe is written for. GetDataProtectionPolicy needs an entry rather than a binding because the topic resource binds ResourceArn, and a probe may not draw on a value the run owns. The phone number is in the 555-0100 to 555-0199 block the North American Numbering Plan reserves for fictional use in every area code, so CheckIfPhoneNumberIsOptedOut asks about nobody.

sqs.$comment: TaskHandle is base64 on AWS — StartMessageMoveTask hands back an opaque encoded handle — so the placeholder is base64 too: an unencoded string is answered with a validation error rather than the not-found the probe is written for. This one decodes to {"taskId":"compat-scenario"}. QueueUrl and SourceArn name a queue in an account that is not the caller's, so a probe of AddPermission, RemovePermission, CancelMessageMoveTask or ListMessageMoveTasks cannot reach the queue the run created.

organizations.$comment: AccountId is the documentation account id, never the caller's: every account-scoped probe names an account this organization does not contain, so the only answer it can get is a not-found.
